name: Paracetamol
commonDosage: Adults: 500mg-1g every 4-6 hours when needed, maximum 4g in 24 hours. Children: 15mg per kg per dose, every 6 hours
sideEffects: Liver damage if the daily maximum is exceeded or taken with heavy alcohol use
contraindications: Careful dosing needed with low body weight, ongoing alcohol misuse or liver problems
pregnancyCategory: Safe at therapeutic doses — first-choice pain and fever medicine in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Ibuprofen
commonDosage: Adults: 200-400mg every 6-8 hours with food, maximum 1.2g in 24 hours without prescription. Children: 5-10mg per kg per dose, every 6-8 hours
sideEffects: Kidney strain, especially in older people or dehydration
Can raise blood pressure and worsen asthma in some people
pregnancyCategory: Avoid, especially from 20 weeks onwards and never in the third trimester
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Aspirin (low-dose)
commonDosage: Heart protection: 75-150mg once daily after food, exactly as prescribed. Pain use (adults): 300-600mg every 4-6 hours, maximum 4g in 24 hours
sideEffects: Ringing in the ears at high doses
contraindications: Children and teenagers with viral illness (risk of Reye's syndrome)
pregnancyCategory: Low-dose only when specifically prescribed for a heart or clotting condition
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Tramadol
commonDosage: Adults: 50-100mg every 4-6 hours for short periods, maximum 400mg in 24 hours; lowest effective dose for the shortest time
sideEffects: Serotonin syndrome when combined with certain antidepressants
Can trigger seizures in people with epilepsy
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — can cause withdrawal in the newborn
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Amoxicillin
commonDosage: Adults: 500mg every 8 hours. Children: 25-50mg per kg per day divided into three doses, as prescribed
contraindications: Penicillin allergy — tell the clinic or pharmacist before collection
pregnancyCategory: Safe — commonly used in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid
commonDosage: Adults: 625mg every 8 hours with food, as prescribed; dose and duration depend on the infection
contraindications: Previous liver problems with this medicine
pregnancyCategory: Safe when needed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Azithromycin
commonDosage: Commonly 500mg on day 1 then 250mg daily for 2-4 days, or a single 1g dose for certain infections — follow the prescribed course exactly
sideEffects: Can affect heart rhythm in people with existing rhythm problems
pregnancyCategory: Generally safe when prescribed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Ciprofloxacin
commonDosage: Adults: 250-750mg every 12 hours depending on the infection, as prescribed
sideEffects: Tendon pain — rarely tendon rupture, mostly in older people
contraindications: Not routinely for children and growing adolescents
Take at least 2 hours apart from antacids, iron or calcium
pregnancyCategory: Avoid
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Metronidazole
commonDosage: Adults: 400mg every 8 hours for 5-7 days, or a single 2g dose for some infections, as prescribed
sideEffects: Severe flushing, vomiting and palpitations if alcohol is taken with it
contraindications: No alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours after the last dose
First trimester of pregnancy for some indications
pregnancyCategory: Used after the first trimester when needed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Cotrimoxazole
commonDosage: Infections: 960mg every 12 hours. Prevention (for example in HIV): 960mg once daily, as prescribed
sideEffects: Rarely severe skin reactions — stop and seek care for any spreading rash with mouth ulcers or fever
contraindications: First trimester and last weeks of pregnancy
pregnancyCategory: Preventive daily dose in HIV continues with folic acid, on clinical advice
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH ART guidelines

name: Doxycycline
commonDosage: Adults: 100mg every 12 hours, swallowed with plenty of water while sitting or standing upright
sideEffects: Sun sensitivity — cover up and use sunscreen
Nausea and irritation of the food pipe if not taken upright with water
contraindications: Children under 8 years for routine use
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — affects developing teeth and bones
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Ceftriaxone
commonDosage: Given as an intramuscular or intravenous injection at the clinic or hospital — commonly 1g daily; dose depends on the infection
contraindications: Not mixed with calcium-containing drips in newborns
pregnancyCategory: Safe when needed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Benzathine benzylpenicillin
commonDosage: Syphilis: 2.4 million units by deep intramuscular injection, single dose (course per stage). Rheumatic fever prevention: monthly injection as prescribed
sideEffects: Rarely a severe allergic reaction — usually within 30 minutes, which is why a short wait after injection is advised
pregnancyCategory: Safe — the treatment of choice for syphilis in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Clotrimazole cream
commonDosage: Apply a thin layer to the affected area 2-3 times daily and continue for 1-2 weeks after the skin clears
sideEffects: Mild burning or stinging when applied
pregnancyCategory: Safe — topical treatment of choice in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Fluconazole
commonDosage: Vaginal thrush: one 150mg capsule. Other fungal infections: daily dosing as prescribed
sideEffects: Rarely liver injury with longer courses
contraindications: Caution with liver disease, and with medicines such as warfarin, phenytoin and gliclazide — interactions are common
pregnancyCategory: A single 150mg dose is considered acceptable; regular dosing is avoided in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Permethrin 5% cream
commonDosage: Apply to the whole body from the neck down (including the head and face in babies) at bedtime, wash off after 8-14 hours; repeat after 7 days. Treat all household contacts and wash bedding and clothes in hot water
sideEffects: Itching may be worse for a few days after treatment
contraindications: Babies under 2 months are treated only on clinical advice
pregnancyCategory: Considered safe in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Oral rehydration solution (ORS)
commonDosage: Dissolve one sachet in 1 litre of clean water exactly as instructed. Adults: drink after every loose stool. Children: 50-100ml per kg over the first 4 hours, plus usual milk or food — small sips frequently if vomiting
sideEffects: None when mixed and given correctly
Vomiting when drunk too quickly — give smaller sips
contraindications: Severe dehydration, repeated vomiting or drowsiness needs clinic assessment — ORS alone is not enough
Never dilute incorrectly or add extra sugar or salt
pregnancyCategory: Safe
source: WHO / UNICEF / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Zinc sulphate
commonDosage: Children with diarrhoea: 20mg once daily for 10-14 days (10mg daily for babies under 6 months), given together with ORS
pregnancyCategory: Not applicable — paediatric use
source: WHO / UNICEF / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Omeprazole
commonDosage: Adults: 20mg once daily in the morning before food, usually for 4-8 weeks; long-term use only under clinical review
sideEffects: Long-term use can lower vitamin B12 and magnesium and slightly raise fracture risk
contraindications: Review with the clinic before continuous use beyond 8 weeks
pregnancyCategory: Acceptable when needed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Metoclopramide
commonDosage: Adults: 10mg every 8 hours for a maximum of 5 days
sideEffects: Rare distressing muscle spasms of the face or neck (more common in young adults)
Long use can cause uncontrollable movements
pregnancyCategory: Only short, prescribed courses
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Loperamide
commonDosage: Adults: 4mg first dose, then 2mg after each loose stool, no more than 16mg in 24 hours and only for short periods
contraindications: Fever or blood in the stool (dysentery)
Not for acute diarrhoea with fever — rehydration is the treatment
pregnancyCategory: Avoid unless advised by a clinician
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Senna
commonDosage: Adults: 7.5-15mg at night, for a few days only
sideEffects: Long-term daily use makes the bowel lazy and drains body salts
contraindications: Sudden tummy pain of unknown cause — get it assessed first
Not for long-term daily use without review
pregnancyCategory: Short-term use acceptable in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Salbutamol inhaler
commonDosage: 1-2 puffs (100-200 micrograms) when needed, up to 4 times daily. Acute wheeze: up to 6 puffs via a spacer, repeated as the clinic or ambulance service advises. Always use a spacer, especially in children
contraindications: None absolute — the reliever must never be withheld in an asthma attack
Using it more than twice a week means the asthma is not controlled: book a clinic review
pregnancyCategory: Safe — asthma control in pregnancy protects the baby
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Beclometasone preventer inhaler
commonDosage: 100-400 micrograms twice daily as prescribed — every day, even when well, with the mouth rinsed after use
sideEffects: Oral thrush and a hoarse voice — preventable by rinsing and using a spacer
Slight growth effect in children at high doses
contraindications: Not for an acute attack — the blue reliever inhaler is for attacks; this is a preventer
pregnancyCategory: Safe — and important to continue in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Prednisone
commonDosage: Asthma or severe allergy flare: commonly 30-40mg once daily for 3-5 days, exactly as prescribed; other conditions have longer courses with gradual tapering
sideEffects: Raised sugar, increased appetite, mood change and poor sleep
Long courses: bone thinning, muscle weakness, high blood pressure, and infections flaring up
Never stop a long course suddenly — the body needs to be weaned off
contraindications: Live vaccines while on high doses
Caution with stomach ulcers and diabetes
pregnancyCategory: Used when clinically needed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Hydrocortisone cream 1%
commonDosage: Apply a thin layer to the affected skin once or twice daily for up to a week (shorter on the face and skin folds)
sideEffects: Skin thinning, stretch marks and pigment change with overuse
Rebound flare when stopped suddenly after long use
contraindications: Infected skin unless the infection is also treated
Not for long-term daily use, and not stronger steroids on the face without advice
pregnancyCategory: Safe for short courses
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Amlodipine
commonDosage: 5mg once daily, may be increased to 10mg once daily as prescribed
contraindications: Severe narrowing of the aortic valve
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — the clinic will switch medicines when pregnancy is planned
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH hypertension guidelines

name: Enalapril
commonDosage: 5-10mg once daily (up to 40mg under supervision), starting low and building up as prescribed
sideEffects: Dizziness with the first doses — take the first dose at bedtime
Raised potassium and kidney function changes
Rarely swelling of the lips or tongue — urgent care if this happens
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — harmful to the unborn baby; effective alternatives exist in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH hypertension guidelines

name: Hydrochlorothiazide
commonDosage: 12.5-25mg once daily in the morning
sideEffects: Passing more urine in the first days
Mildly raised sugar and sun sensitivity
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — particularly near delivery
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH hypertension guidelines

name: Furosemide
commonDosage: 20-40mg once daily in the morning (higher doses only under hospital supervision)
sideEffects: Ringing in the ears with rapid injection
pregnancyCategory: Only under specialist care
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Atenolol
commonDosage: 25-50mg once daily, as prescribed
sideEffects: Tiredness and cold hands and feet
Can mask the warning signs of a low sugar in people on diabetes medicines
contraindications: Asthma — discuss with the clinic before use
Severe slow pulse or heart block
Never stop suddenly — taper as instructed
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — alternatives are preferred in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH hypertension guidelines

name: Simvastatin
commonDosage: 10-40mg once at night (maximum 40mg; maximum 20mg if also taking amlodipine)
sideEffects: Muscle aches — report severe muscle pain, weakness or dark urine urgently
Raised liver enzymes on blood tests
pregnancyCategory: Avoid
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Metformin
commonDosage: Start 500mg once or twice daily with food, building to 1g twice daily as prescribed; maximum 2.55g daily in divided doses
sideEffects: Nausea, runny tummy and a metallic taste — usually settle in the first weeks
Vitamin B12 deficiency over many years
Rarely lactic acidosis during severe illness with dehydration — sick-day rules apply
contraindications: Temporarily paused during serious illness, dehydration or scans with contrast dye — clinic will advise
pregnancyCategory: Safe — commonly continued in pregnancy, with insulin added where needed
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH diabetes guidelines

name: Gliclazide
commonDosage: 40-80mg once daily with breakfast, increased as prescribed up to 160mg twice daily
sideEffects: Low sugar — shaking, sweating, confusion; treat with fast sugar and review the dose at the clinic
contraindications: Skipped meals make low sugar more likely — never take without eating
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — insulin is used in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH diabetes guidelines

name: Insulin (human)
commonDosage: Fully individualised — commonly started around 0.4-0.6 units per kg body weight per day in split doses, and adjusted by the clinic based on readings
sideEffects: Low sugar if doses are missed around meals or activity changes
Injection-site lumps if sites are not rotated
contraindications: None absolute — insulin is life-saving in type 1 diabetes
Doses must be adjusted during illness; never skip insulin when sick without clinic guidance
pregnancyCategory: Safe — the standard treatment for diabetes in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH diabetes guidelines

name: Warfarin
commonDosage: Dose is individualised and adjusted to the INR blood test (usually targeting 2.0-3.0, higher for some mechanical valves) — take the exact prescribed dose at the same time daily
sideEffects: Bleeding — gums, nose, heavy bruises, blood in urine or stool (urgent care)
Rarely skin necrosis at the start
contraindications: Unsupervised use in pregnancy — specialist care only
Many interactions: antibiotics, antifungals, pain medicines and traditional remedies can swing the INR — always tell the clinic and pharmacist
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — specialist alternatives are used in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Levothyroxine
commonDosage: Individualised, commonly 25-100 micrograms once daily; take on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast with water only
sideEffects: Too high a dose: palpitations, weight loss, tremor, poor sleep and bone thinning over time
contraindications: Recent heart attack — start cautiously as directed
pregnancyCategory: Safe — and the dose usually needs to increase in pregnancy; never stop it
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Amitriptyline
commonDosage: Nerve pain or migraine prevention: 10-25mg at night. Depression: higher doses under clinical supervision
sideEffects: Drowsiness — take at night; avoid driving until the effect is known
Weight gain and urinary difficulty in older men
contraindications: Recent heart attack or heart rhythm problems
Caution in older people — falls risk
pregnancyCategory: Avoid unless clearly needed — discuss with the clinic
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Fluoxetine
commonDosage: 20mg once daily in the morning (may be increased to 40mg under supervision); improvement usually shows after 2-4 weeks — do not stop suddenly
sideEffects: Nausea, headache and brief anxiety in the first days
Serotonin syndrome when combined with tramadol or similar medicines — report agitation, fever and tremor urgently
contraindications: Manic episodes in the past — specialist supervision
pregnancyCategory: One of the better-studied antidepressants — planned use in pregnancy is coordinated with the clinic
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Carbamazepine
commonDosage: Start 100-200mg once or twice daily, building as prescribed to a usual range of 800-1200mg daily in divided doses
sideEffects: Dizziness, drowsiness and blurred vision — often settle as the body adjusts
Any rash must be reported immediately — rare severe skin reactions
Low sodium and blood count changes on long-term blood monitoring
contraindications: Weakens oral contraceptives — extra contraception needed
pregnancyCategory: Raises birth-defect risk — pregnancy planning is coordinated with the clinic, with folic acid before conception
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Phenytoin
commonDosage: Commonly 300mg once daily, adjusted to blood levels — take consistently, and never change dose without the clinic
sideEffects: Unsteadiness and jerky eye movements when the level is high
Coarsening of facial features over many years
contraindications: Many interactions — antibiotics and antifungals can push levels dangerously high
pregnancyCategory: Raises birth-defect risk — specialist planning with folic acid before conception
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Sodium valproate
commonDosage: 500mg-1g daily in divided doses, individualised and monitored
sideEffects: Liver injury — children under 2 are at highest risk
Polycystic ovary features in some women
contraindications: Pregnancy, or the possibility of pregnancy, unless a specialist has approved a specific plan — this medicine carries the highest birth-defect risk of the older seizure medicines
pregnancyCategory: Avoid — the highest-risk seizure medicine in pregnancy; effective alternatives exist
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Allopurinol
commonDosage: Start 100mg once daily and build up as prescribed (commonly 300mg daily; lower with kidney problems)
sideEffects: Rash — any rash must be reported urgently (rare severe skin reactions)
Gout may flare when starting — preventive cover is often given
contraindications: Do not start for the first time alone during an acute gout flare — flares are managed first, on clinical advice
pregnancyCategory: Avoid unless essential
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Ferrous sulphate
commonDosage: Adults: one tablet (about 60mg of iron) once or twice daily. Children: 3-6mg of iron per kg per day. Take with water or a vitamin C drink, on an empty stomach if tolerated
contraindications: Iron overload conditions such as haemochromatosis
Separate from levothyroxine, antacids and calcium by at least 4 hours
Tea, coffee and milk within an hour block absorption
pregnancyCategory: Safe — routinely given in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Folic acid
commonDosage: Preventing birth defects: 400-500 micrograms daily from before pregnancy through the first trimester. Deficiency or high-risk pregnancy: 5mg daily as prescribed
contraindications: Untreated vitamin B12 deficiency — folic acid can mask the anaemia while nerve damage continues; B12 is checked first
pregnancyCategory: Essential in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH Standard Treatment Guidelines

name: Artemether-lumefantrine
commonDosage: Adults (35kg and over): 4 tablets at 0, 8, 24, 36, 48 and 60 hours — 24 tablets in total; children are dosed by weight. Always take with food or milk containing fat
contraindications: Malaria with danger signs (confusion, fits, inability to drink) — this is emergency hospital treatment
Caution with other medicines affecting heart rhythm
Rifampicin and epilepsy medicines can make it fail — the clinic chooses the antimalarial accordingly
pregnancyCategory: Used for malaria treatment, with clinician guidance in the first trimester — untreated malaria is more dangerous
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH malaria guidelines / WHO

name: TLD (fixed-dose ART)
commonDosage: One tablet once daily, at the same time every day, with or without food
sideEffects: Mild sleep and dream changes in the first weeks
Weight gain over the first year
Rare kidney effects from tenofovir — blood tests monitor this
Antacids, iron and calcium supplements block absorption of the dolutegravir part — separate by at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after
contraindications: Rifampicin for TB requires dose adjustment — managed by the clinic
pregnancyCategory: Safe — the standard first-line regimen in South Africa, including in pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH ART guidelines

name: TB combination (RHZE)
commonDosage: Weight-banded daily fixed-dose combination for the first 2 months, followed by rifampicin-isoniazid for 4 months — the full course is six months
sideEffects: Orange-red urine, sweat and tears — normal and expected
Liver injury — report yellow eyes, dark urine or severe nausea the same day
Vision changes or difficulty telling colours apart (ethambutol) — same-day care
Vitamin B6 is usually given alongside to protect the nerves
contraindications: Jaundice or severe liver disease — managed by the TB unit
Rifampicin weakens oral contraceptives, warfarin and many other medicines — always tell every provider that TB treatment is being taken
pregnancyCategory: Used in pregnancy under the national TB programme, with vitamin B6
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH TB guidelines

name: Adrenaline 1:1000 injection
commonDosage: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis): adults 0.5mg (0.5ml) injected into the outer thigh muscle; children 0.01mg per kg, maximum 0.5mg. Repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement — and always call 10177
sideEffects: Fast heartbeat, tremor, pallor and anxiety — expected and temporary
The life-saving benefit far outweighs these effects in anaphylaxis
contraindications: None in anaphylaxis — delay is the greater danger
This is first aid while the ambulance is on the way, not a replacement for hospital care
pregnancyCategory: Use without delay in anaphylaxis at any stage of pregnancy
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA Resuscitation Council

name: Methyldopa
commonDosage: 250mg two to three times daily (up to 2-3g daily in divided doses), as prescribed
sideEffects: Drowsiness and dizziness in the first days — usually settles
Rarely liver changes — blood tests monitor this
contraindications: History of depression — discuss with the clinic
pregnancyCategory: Safe — a first-choice blood pressure medicine in pregnancy in South Africa
source: SA Essential Medicines List / SA NDoH maternity care guidelines
